articles.title: NATO defense spending shifts toward AI, drones - Daily Tribune
articles.summary: NATO defense spending shifts toward AI, drones  Daily Tribune
articles.full_text:
NATO is preparing a new defense strategy centered on drones, artificial intelligence and other emerging technologies, signaling a potential shift in how member states allocate military spending as the alliance prepares for a possible Russian attack on its eastern flank.
The strategy, known as the “Theory of Victory,” is being developed by Supreme Allied Commander Europe General Alexus Grynkewich and is expected to be presented in Poland on 12 October.
Beyond its military implications, the plan highlights the growing role of technology in defense procurement as NATO members increase spending and assess alternatives to traditional weapons systems.
The proposed strategy would combine conventional forces with low-cost drones, minimally crewed systems and AI-enabled targeting. NATO would use these capabilities alongside land forces to block a potential incursion and, if necessary, disrupt enemy command-and-control systems.
Colonel Martin O’Donnell, a spokesman for Grynkewich, said the alliance’s objective is to maintain its military advantage while deterring aggression.
“The Supreme Allied Commander Europe’s theory of victory is simple: maintain NATO’s advantage,” O’Donnell said. “Given the unsettled and complex global security environment, we need to set conditions now to deter aggression and, if necessary, win if attacked.”
The strategy comes as European NATO members ramp up defense budgets and debate how much funding should go toward conventional equipment such as tanks versus newer technologies that have gained prominence during the war in Ukraine.
The document also calls for stronger collective defenses against hybrid threats, including hostile activities that fall below the threshold of conventional warfare.
The United States has separately asked NATO allies about additional forces they could contribute to Grynkewich’s defense plans as Washington reviews its military commitments in Europe.
The growing emphasis on AI and autonomous or minimally crewed systems could further accelerate demand for defense technology, potentially reshaping procurement priorities and investment across NATO’s military-industrial sector.

articles.title: UK warships to enter South China Sea despite China protest - UK Defence Journal
articles.summary: UK warships to enter South China Sea despite China protest  UK Defence Journal
articles.full_text:
Royal Navy patrol ships HMS Spey and HMS Tamar are to enter the South China Sea for a ten-day multinational exercise with Australia, Malaysia, New Zealand and Singapore, continuing a British naval presence in waters where Beijing has repeatedly objected to UK military activity and policy, according to the Royal Navy.
The two Batch 2 River-class offshore patrol vessels will take part in Exercise Bersama Lima 26, the annual tri-service exercise conducted under the Five Power Defence Arrangements, or FPDA, which links the United Kingdom with Australia, Malaysia, New Zealand and Singapore.
Bersama Lima, meaning “Together Five” in Malay, will involve ships, aircraft and troops operating across maritime, land and air scenarios. Forces committed to the exercise include frigates, patrol vessels, a corvette, tanker and submarine, as well as divers and specialist boarding teams.
Australian F-35A Lightning II fighters will lead the air element of the exercise, while planned scenarios include troops directing naval gunfire, boarding and searching vessels at sea, anti-submarine warfare and naval air defence supported by participating air forces.
The deployment takes place against a long-running dispute between Beijing and several regional governments over territorial and maritime claims in the South China Sea, as well as wider disagreements over the activities of military forces from countries outside the region. China has repeatedly criticised British involvement. In 2018, Beijing said it had lodged stern representations with the UK after HMS Albion sailed close to the Paracel Islands, which China calls the Xisha Islands. China said the ship had entered waters it regarded as its territorial sea without permission, while Britain has consistently maintained the importance of navigational rights under international law.
Beijing again objected in 2021 as the UK increased its naval presence in the Indo-Pacific, accusing Britain of deploying its Carrier Strike Group to the South China Sea to “flex its naval muscles”. More recently, in July 2026, the Chinese Embassy in London strongly condemned the UK for joining an international statement supporting the 2016 South China Sea arbitration award and urged Britain to stop what it described as “stirring up trouble” in the region.
HMS Tamar has also recently conducted a freedom-of-navigation activity in the South China Sea. In a parliamentary answer published on 8 September, the Ministry of Defence confirmed that the patrol ship operated alongside the Royal Australian Navy on 1 September as part of the UK’s stated commitment to freedom of navigation and overflight under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea.
The Royal Navy says HMS Spey and HMS Tamar have themselves conducted freedom-of-navigation missions in disputed waters during their five-year deployment to the Indo-Pacific, sometimes operating independently and sometimes alongside regional partners.
Before Bersama Lima moves into its main operational phase, personnel from the five participating nations will spend time familiarising themselves with different vessels, equipment, procedures and terminology, while senior officers carry out planning for the live exercise.
According to a Royal Navy news update, Lieutenant Commander Cheryl Goodwin, HMS Tamar’s Executive Officer, said: “We’re looking forward to being a part of Bersama Lima 26 – an exercise which unites some of our closest allies, tests the crew in a traditional war-fighting role, and demonstrates the UK’s resolve to maintain stability in the Indo-Pacific region through supporting our partners.”
HMS Tamar is also carrying a Royal New Zealand Navy boarding team during the exercise, adding another element of direct integration between the participating forces.
Lieutenant Williams, a Royal New Zealand Navy officer embarked aboard Tamar, said: “It’s a first for me and my team, but it’s a well-trodden path which has been established through a deep history of our navies working together.”
He added: “We’ve got a lot of experience to share, are always looking to improve and we’re ready to go.”
The Five Power Defence Arrangements were established in 1971 and provide a framework for defence cooperation between the five member states. Regular exercises bring together naval, land and air forces, particularly around Malaysia and Singapore, to practise combined operations and develop common procedures. Both British patrol ships have been forward deployed to the Indo-Pacific since 2021. Their mission, known as Operation Highwall, has included multinational exercises, maritime security operations, sanctions enforcement, humanitarian assistance, defence engagement and freedom-of-navigation activity.
Bersama Lima marks a return to operations for HMS Spey after the vessel spent the summer undergoing maintenance in Singapore. HMS Tamar has remained active across the region, including participation in the US-led Pacific Partnership humanitarian exercise and a visit to Cambodia before its September activity with the Royal Australian Navy in the South China Sea.
The ships passed five years continuously deployed to the Indo-Pacific in September, making them the first Royal Navy vessels to maintain a persistent presence in the region since the handover of Hong Kong in 1997.
During Bersama Lima, Spey and Tamar will operate as part of a larger multinational force, with the live phase testing the five FPDA nations across areas including maritime interdiction, anti-submarine warfare and air defence in and around the South China Sea.
Tamar and Spey have often entered the South China seas without much of a peep from Beijing. It’s when they undertake highly publicised exercises or call it a FONOPS in the media, that’s when Beijing gets miffed. When Spey went through the Taiwan Straits last year, IIRC it wasn’t the passage that China objected to. It was the UK Government’s rhetoric. Sure there’s shadowing sometimes, as we might do to them, but top level protests are rare.
If we had more frigates, I’d rather we used them for the SCS exercises and the publicised FONOPS, and let the two OPVs quietly go about their business. The are not warships – not ships of war, anyway. Calling them that in a provocative context isn’t helpful. Of course we don’t have any more frigates, so the B2s will have to do. If they are pulled back to patrol the English Channel next year, we won’t have any ships in the Far East at all.
A frigate wouldn’t be any better off than an OPV facing China’s A2AD bubble. But then attacking them would amount to a declaration of war. The point is to demonstrate skin in the game, which the OPVs do adequately.
They are barely armed patrol ships, not warships.
This is why the RN needs an urgent second batch of type 31s. We are tasking patrol ships with tasks a warship should be doing.

articles.title: Warlock Ransomware Group Expands SharePoint Attacks on Critical Infrastructure Across Latin America and Iberia - Computer Crime Research Center
articles.summary: Warlock Ransomware Group Expands SharePoint Attacks on Critical Infrastructure Across Latin America and Iberia  Computer Crime Research Center
articles.full_text:
Security researchers reported that a China-based threat group known as Warlock has been exploiting vulnerabilities in Microsoft SharePoint, including the “ToolShell” flaws disclosed in 2025 along with newer bugs patched in 2026, to break into critical infrastructure operators across Spanish- and Portuguese-speaking countries. According to reporting by The Record and other outlets, confirmed victims include a water utility, a telecommunications provider, a university and a regional government agency, with the campaign spanning targets across Europe, Africa and Latin America.
Once inside a network, the attackers reportedly conduct extensive reconnaissance before deploying tools designed to disable endpoint security products across multiple hosts, then install additional utilities built to blend in with legitimate administrator activity and avoid detection. Researchers at Symantec, cited in the reporting, said the group previously relied on the LockBit ransomware strain before switching to its own Warlock payload, and that unpatched SharePoint servers remain the primary entry point for the ongoing intrusions.
Microsoft has said it cannot tie the Chinese actors behind Warlock to any other state-sponsored group it already tracks, leaving open the question of whether the operation is financially motivated cybercrime, state-linked espionage, or some blend of the two, a distinction that has grown increasingly blurry among China-nexus hacking crews. The group has reportedly been active since before 2025 and has previously struck targets in the United States, Russia, Brazil, India, Taiwan and Japan.

articles.title: ⚡ Weekly Recap: NetScaler and FortiMail 0-Days, AI Coding Leaks, Spectre v2 and Ransomware Arrests - The Hacker News
articles.summary: ⚡ Weekly Recap: NetScaler and FortiMail 0-Days, AI Coding Leaks, Spectre v2 and Ransomware Arrests  The Hacker News
articles.full_text:
A blank field. A public repo. One reply to an email. A box left exposed. None of this sounds dramatic, which is partly the problem. This week’s threats keep finding leverage in small things that were easy to overlook.
There are actively exploited bugs in the mix, cleaner intrusion paths, smarter automation, and a long patch list waiting behind them. Some attacks are getting more capable. Others are still getting in because the basics gave way first.
Here’s what mattered this week.
Citrix Warns of Newly Exploited NetScaler ADC and Gateway Flaw — Citrix released security updates for a high-severity security flaw in NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway that has been exploited as part of targeted zero-day attacks. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-88779, carries a CVSS score of 8.7 out of 10.0. "CVE-2026-88779 is a memory overflow vulnerability in Citrix NetScaler ADC and Citrix NetScaler Gateway that can lead to denial-of-service under specific deployment conditions," Citrix said. "The issue affects customer-managed NetScaler deployments running affected supported versions when the required preconditions are met." Successful exploitation requires NetScaler ADC or NetScaler Gateway to be configured either as a SAML service provider (SP) or SAML identity provider(IdP).
Most teams are stuck choosing between speed and control. Headspace found a way to have both. Hear how Chris Oh, Senior Director of AI Enablement at Headspace, gives the org flexibility to build, while maintaining full visibility into what’s running and who owns it.
Watch the On-Demand Webinar Here ➝
- Critical FortiMail Zero-Day Flaw Exploited in Attacks — The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) warned of active exploitation of a critical security flaw impacting Fortinet FortiMail. The flaw, CVE-2026-104286 (CVSS score: 9.8), allows unauthenticated attackers to write arbitrary files on the underlying system. According to Fortinet, the vulnerability "may allow an unauthenticated attacker to write arbitrary files on the underlying system via crafted HTTP or HTTPS requests."
- Two ShinyHunters Members Arrested — Law enforcement agencies have arrested two members associated with the ShinyHunters digital extortion group. One of them is a 24-year-old Amsterdam man, who is believed to be Pepijn van der Stap, while the second individual is Saif al-Din Khader, who is said to have been detained by Jordanian authorities last week. ShinyHunters has drawn attention in recent weeks for hijacking the darknet website of Cl0p and its hack of the FBI's "apply.fbijobs[.]gov" portal.
- Authorities Arrest 16-Year-Old Mastermind Behind KillSec — Police in Spain apprehended a 16-year-old who is suspected to be the leader of the KillSec (aka Kill Security Ransomware Group) ransomware operation.
According to Europol, authorities took control of KillSec's leak site on September 30, 2026, securing no less than 110 terabytes of data.
As part of Operation KillSwitch, a total of three suspects were provisionally arrested and eight properties searched in Greece, Romania, Spain, and the U.
K.
One of the group’s accused members, Fouad Eltibrizi, was arrested in the U.
K.
and is awaiting extradition to the U.
S.
Since emerging in 2024, the group is estimated to have launched around 1,000 attacks, at least half of which were successful.
"The group exploited software vulnerabilities and poorly secured access points, particularly to cloud storage, to gain access to organizations' systems," Europol said.
"Its members then copied sensitive internal data to infrastructure under their control.
Victims were named on the group's dark web leak site and threatened with publication of their data unless paid.
" Per Group-IB, which identified 274 publicly claimed victims, out of which most were U.
S.
, Indian, and Brazilian organizations.
"The group also sold stolen data outright, with asking prices ranging from USD 5,000 for a single company's records to USD 500,000 for the data it claimed to have taken from the global insurer, making KillSec as much a data broker as a ransomware operator," Group-IB said.

- New Spectre v2 Variant Leaks Linux Root Password Hash in Minutes — A new Spectre v2 attack variant called Branch Target Reuse (BTR) can recover root password hashes from Intel computers running Linux in just a few minutes. The attack exploits stale information in a processor's branch predictor after a just-in-time (JIT) engine reuses memory for new code. By tampering with this information, an attacker can trick the processor into temporarily executing wrong instructions and potentially expose sensitive data. "We evaluated the end-to-end exploit on both Raptor Cove and Lion Cove, and leaked the password within 3 and 5 minutes on average, respectively," researchers claimed. "Indirect branch prediction is inherent to modern CPUs, and BTR exploits the desynchronization between the branch predictor and the actual state of the code. No current CPU has a mechanism to keep the two in sync, so until vendors add one, your CPU is vulnerable."
- Star Blizzard Uses Fake Invites to Deploy CosmicPulse — The Russian state-sponsored threat actor known as Star Blizzard has employed a new malware delivery technique called RedFlick in attacks targeting Ukrainian individuals and institutions as well as international non-government organizations (NGOs), Western think tanks, governments, and other organizations associated with international policy. The end goal is to deploy a custom backdoor called CosmicPulse by setting up scheduled tasks using RedFlick through phishing emails masquerading as invitations. Once a victim responds to an initial phishing email, Star Blizzard typically sends a follow-up containing a password-protected archive that triggers the RedFlick chain. "This technique is a notable departure from the actor’s previous use of ClickFix-based infection chains which required victims to complete multiple actions before CosmicPulse could be installed," Microsoft said. "By contrast, the RedFlick infection flow only requires a single user interaction, reducing friction in the compromise process."
- NeedyMantis Malware Enables Persistent Network Access — A modular post-compromise malware family called NeedyMantis is being used by threat actors to maintain long-term stealth access and support post-compromise operations. Distributed by a two-stage loader and launched via DLL sideloading, the malware has been observed in a limited number of targeted operations affecting telecommunications organizations, universities, medical nonprofits, intergovernmental organizations, and government contractors. The activity aligns with operations that are associated with threat actors operating from China. The malware operation has been active since at least October 2025. "While NeedyMantis employs techniques commonly used by modern malware, its architecture combines multiple loaders, custom encrypted file archives, a custom executable file format, and modular components that enable operators to evade analysis and extend functionality through additional modules," Microsoft said. At least one threat actor has been linked to its use: Storm-3069, which is Microsoft's designation for the DAEMON Tools supply chain attack that took place in May 2026.
- RatHat Android Malware Console Uses Gemini to Identify Higher-Value Victims — The Android malware known as RatHat has been observed using Google Gemini to estimate each victim's bank balance and sorts the device into high-value and mid-value groups. "Gemini is used on both sides of the operation: the malware asks an LLM where to tap when its automation fails on an unfamiliar phone, and the panel uses one to estimate victims' bank balances from their SMS," Cleafy said. Over the course of the operation, the threat actors behind RatHat changed its command-and-control (C2) panel entirely, moving from ackCat to Panda Workshop. "The panel works as a complete malware factory: it builds, signs, and publishes new samples from the console, rebuilds them on a schedule to evade hash-based detection, without the operator touching the hosting infrastructure," Cleafy added. "Account caps and role-gated sections exist to constrain the panel's own users, and pivoting on its frontend artifacts resolves the three generations to nearly 100 separate deployments since April 2026."
- AI Coding Agents Leaked 13K Internal Company Screenshots — A new report from Glow Labs found that AI coding agents posted more than 13,000 sensitive screenshots of corporate software projects from 343 companies to public GitHub repositories. The activity has been codenamed PixelLeak. About a third of the exposures came from developers who were using gitshot. "Each case investigated during our 'PixelLeak' research started with a developer asking an agent to prove that a visual change worked," researchers said. "The software was changed, for example with a fix to the user interface layout, and the reviewers needed to see the before and after. The agents figured out that they could make the image available to the human reviewer by hosting it in an adjacent public repo. They just didn't consider the security implications." These incidents show that AI creates new security risks even without having to facilitate cyber attacks.
Bugs drop weekly, and the gap between a patch and an exploit is shrinking fast. These are the heavy hitters for the week: high-severity, widely used, or already being poked at in the wild.

Germany is in a "shadow war" with Russia and risks being drawn into a violent conflict with Moscow, Martin Jaeger, head of the foreign intelligence service (BND), told lawmakers during a Parliamentary Control Committee hearing on Oct. 5.
"No other country currently poses such a direct, comprehensive, and concrete threat to Germany," Jaeger said during the public hearing, in reference to the attempted Russian drone attack at Leipzig airport on July 31.
"Russia is waging a shadow war against us," Jaeger said further, meaning an undeclared war that cannot be grasped by conventional military or judicial understandings of the term.
Jaeger warned of further sabotage and nuclear intimidation by Moscow to ensure that no measures against Russia would be taken in Berlin or other European capitals, and to halt support and arms deliveries for Ukraine.
Calling the Russian intelligence services "highly professional and reckless," Jaeger also said that the threat of Russian attacks on targets in Germany remains "real and present."
Jaeger said the BND does not currently see signs of a large-scale Russian attack on NATO territory, but warned of low-level Russian military activity, especially in the Baltic region.
Sinan Selen, head of the internal federal intelligence service (BfV), also said that Russia was willing to carry out sabotage and assassinations.
Martina Rosenberg, head of the military intelligence service (MAD), added that the German military was facing enemies from outside, as well as from within.
All three intelligence chiefs called for reforms of their agencies, allowing them to operate in more offensive capacities, such as against cyberattacks or to sabotage adversarial weapons programs.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz arrived in Kyiv on Oct. 4 for a visit aimed at reaffirming Berlin's support for Ukraine, the German news agency dpa reported.
Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said he welcomed Merz to Kyiv on Sunday morning and that the chancellor would hold talks with President Volodymyr Zelensky on bilateral relations, European affairs, and international issues.

President Volodymyr Zelensky warned on Sunday, Oct. 4, that Ukraine has responded and will continue to deliver proportional retaliatory strikes against Russian infrastructure.
Speaking during a joint press briefing with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz in Kyiv, Zelensky questioned the strategic calculations behind Moscow’s intensifying strikes on civilian utilities, warning that critical Russian facilities – including telecommunications backbones in Moscow – remain vulnerable to reciprocal Ukrainian deep strikes.
“Honestly, I am not surprised by such an approach to war – hatred toward Ukraine from Russia. But I am surprised by this specific approach, because they struck our warehouses: Nova Poshta, Ukrposhta, and others. They struck, and we gave them a worthy response against Wildberries,” Zelensky told reporters.
“Now they are striking bridges. Do they really think we will not respond?”
Symmetrical response
Zelensky highlighted that Russian forces have expanded strikes against Ukrainian civilian life-support systems, deliberately directing loitering munitions and ballistic missiles against corporate data centers and mobile telecommunications installations.
The president warned that such actions establish a precedent for reciprocal targeting, reminding Moscow that its own infrastructure operates under identical vulnerabilities.
“Does [Russian President Vladimir] Putin not realize that mobile communications are used not only in Kyiv, in Ukraine? They are used in Moscow as well,” Zelensky said.
“I am simply, honestly, surprised by this beastly desire to escalate every day. That is, he relies on continuous escalation; he wants this very much. This is an answer to all those who believe that one just needs to simply ask Putin and he will definitely end the war. It simply will not work.”
Zelensky emphasized that Moscow’s conduct demonstrates that the Russian leadership does not seek diplomatic off-ramps, but instead uses aerial barrages to compel political concessions through intimidation ahead of the winter heating season.
Consecutive strikes on Kyiv bridges
The president’s warning follows two consecutive days of Russian strikes targeting Kyiv’s North Bridge, compounding structural strain across the capital’s metropolitan transport network.
Earlier on Sunday morning, Russian munitions struck the road deck of the North Bridge for the second time in 24 hours, blasting a crater into the asphalt roadway spanning the Dnipro River.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko reported that emergency services and transit engineers deployed immediately to assess structural integrity, confirming that two civilians sustained injuries in the Sunday attack, with one hospitalized and a second treated on-site.
The Sunday bombardment followed a direct hit on Saturday morning, Oct. 3, when a Russian turbojet loitering munition struck the North Bridge, damaging the road surface and severing overhead electrical contact wires powering municipal trolleybuses.
The consecutive hits on the North Bridge follow the complete closure of the capital’s South Bridge to vehicular traffic on Friday after repeated drone impacts damaged roadway spans, bridge piers, and structural barriers shielding the Green Line metro crossing.

articles.full_text:
The world is facing a record-breaking El Nino this year, and weather experts say governments need to prepare now as 'death and severe illness' are on the cards
Weather experts are urging governments across the world to “act now” as El Nino is set to intensify significantly before the end of the year.
El Nino occurs every few years when temperatures in the tropical eastern Pacific rise 0.5C above the long-term average. For the UK, it tends to lead to wetter and stormier conditions in the winter months, and extreme heat during the summer.
Experts say the current El Nino is likely to be the strongest in living memory. Celeste Saulo, Secretary-General of the World Meteorological Organization (WMO), says “we still have time to act” and called on health authorities across the world to treat extreme heat “as the predictable public-health risk that it is”.
Much of the Southern Hemisphere will face its hottest months at the start of 2027, just as El Nino will be peaking. The WMO says “death and severe illness” are on the cards as the extreme conditions will exacerbate preexisting health conditions.
But the heat isn’t the only risk. Armel Castellan, Extreme Heat Advisor from the WHO-WMO Climate and Health Joint Programme, says: “WMO’s seasonal climate outlook for September to November points to above-normal rainfall in some regions and drought risk in others. That puts water security, nutrition, and vector-borne disease on the table alongside temperature.
“The WMO seasonal outlooks buy us much needed lead time, and that lead time is what lets health authorities look ahead and prepare, rather than repair. If health practitioners can make informed decisions, this can make the difference between losing lives or saving them.”

Warmer temperatures and changing rainfall patterns also bring an increased risk of diseases carried by mosquitoes, the WMO says. Malaria, dengue, chikungunya, yellow fever and Zika could all spread to regions where they are not usually seen.
The WMO identified malnutrition and cholera as among the “most serious concerns” in regions facing both drought and flooding. Moreover, the amount of people facing acute food insecurity is expected to rise - and it already stands at 150 million globally.
Teresa Zakaria, Unit Head for Risk Reduction, Humanitarian Operations and Climate Change at WHO, said: “El Nino is a significant public health threat, not just a climate phenomenon. It is a risk multiplier, and we expect to see health impacts across the world.
“However, the most severe impacts will be experienced where climate shocks intersect with weak health systems, limited access to health care, food insecurity, displacement and humanitarian crises.”

articles.full_text:
European defense technology startups are on track to raise $10.5 billion in venture capital by the end of 2026 — nearly four times the $2.6 billion raised across all of 2025 — according to a new State of Defence Tech 2026 report published Monday by market intelligence firm Dealroom and defense media outlet Resilience Media, timed to the opening of the Resilience Conference in London. Defense now accounts for 11.1 percent of all European venture capital investment, up from 4 percent just one year ago.
The scale of the shift is historically without parallel. As recently as 2021, a $113 million Series A from a Munich-based startup called Helsing was enough to set a new European defense tech funding record. Five years later, Helsing raised $1.8 billion Series E on July 13 at an $18 billion valuation — the largest private funding round ever raised by a European defense firm and the largest by any German startup on record. Eleven days earlier, fellow Munich company Quantum Systems had closed a $1.2 billion Series D at an $8 billion valuation, itself a record that held for less than two weeks. Together the two companies account for more than $25 billion in combined valuation and have helped turn Munich into the undisputed capital of European defense venture.
What Munich Built — and Why Software Is the Answer
What makes Munich's dominance significant is not just the money but the thesis: both Helsing and Quantum Systems are betting that the future of European defense is software-defined rather than hardware-defined, and that the Ukraine war has validated that bet in a way no controlled exercise could.
Helsing describes itself as an artificial intelligence company that happens to build weapons rather than a weapons company that happens to use AI. Its architecture reflects that framing. The company's flagship strike platform, the HX-2 strike drone system, is an electrically propelled x-wing drone weighing approximately 12 kilograms (about 26 pounds) with a range of up to 100 kilometers (62 miles). Its defining technical feature is GPS-independent AI navigation system: the drone's onboard computer runs AI algorithms that use visual landmark recognition to determine its position in real time, without requiring a continuous data link or satellite navigation signal. Because GPS jamming — one of Russia's most effective electronic warfare tools in Ukraine — cannot disrupt the HX-2's position-fixing system, the drone remains theoretically operable in the densely contested electromagnetic environment that has neutralized many conventionally navigated systems.
The HX-2 is integrated with Helsing's Altra AI swarm platform, which enables a single human operator to control multiple drones simultaneously, coordinating swarm operations against armored targets. The company currently produces more than 1,000 of these systems per month from a facility in southern Germany and positions the HX-2 as a lower-cost, mass-deployable complement to conventional artillery and cruise missiles.
Quantum Systems operates in a complementary and deliberately non-lethal lane. Investor restrictions bar the company from developing weapons; its Vector and Trinity electric vertical takeoff and landing (eVTOL) drones are designed exclusively for intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (ISR) — providing the battlefield awareness on which strike systems like the HX-2 then act. The company's CEO, Florian Seibel, a former German army pilot, has been explicit about the goal: make the front line transparent in real time, so that every decision is informed rather than guessed. Quantum Systems produced up to 4,000 drones per year before this funding round and expects to expand that significantly with the $1.2 billion now in hand.
Who Is Funding European Sovereignty — and the Paradox That Entails
There is a structural irony embedded in the European defense tech boom that the headline numbers tend to obscure. The entire investment thesis rests on the premise of European strategic autonomy — the idea that the continent must build its own defense capability without dependence on American suppliers, American intelligence, or American decisions about when and whether to honor alliance commitments. Yet for the first time in the history of European defense venture capital, investors from outside Europe are putting more money into European defense startups than European backers are.
American funds including Lightspeed Venture Partners and General Catalyst led or co-led the Helsing Series E. Bessemer Venture Partners, also American, has made European defense resilience tech one of its active investment categories. Of the $27.1 billion raised across NATO-wide defense VC totals in 2026 to date, the United States alone accounts for $19.6 billion — and a significant portion of the capital flowing into European defense startups traces back to the same American investor class.
Alex Ferrara, a London-based partner at Bessemer Venture Partners resilience investing, frames this not as a contradiction but as a structural fact about where defense investment expertise currently lives. "Lack of exits is indeed an issue here in Europe, but I think it's a problem in the US as well," Ferrara told Resilience Media. "One issue is that, unlike categories of enterprise software where there are many acquirers, in defense tech there are only a small number of strategic acquirers. This is both the opportunity and the challenge."
The exit scarcity is real and documented. Across NATO and allied countries, just 21 defense-tech exits were recorded in all of 2025, compared with an average of eight per year between 2021 and 2024. The defense tech exit data 2026 shows a total exit value of $18.6 billion in 2025, projected at $15.4 billion for 2026. Of the ten largest all-time defense tech exits, only one — London-based quantum encryption company Arqit, which went public via Arqit SPAC 2021 valuation at a $1.4 billion valuation — is European. Ferrara's thesis is that a new generation of "neo-primes" — European defense companies that grow large enough to become acquirers themselves — could eventually solve this, but that the market is not yet deep enough to sustain the volume of exits the current funding pace implies.
Drones Lead, But the Landscape Extends
By technology category, the Dealroom report shows drone investment by category reaching $4.7 billion across 40 European funding rounds in 2026, the highest of any segment. Anti-drone technologies — the defensive side of the same arms race — drew $1.2 billion, while maritime robotics (unmanned surface and underwater vessels) attracted approximately $800 million.
Beyond the Munich pair, other significant European defense companies also raised substantial capital. Portugal's Tekever, which builds AI-enabled autonomous drones that have flown ISR missions in Ukraine and holds a contract with Britain's Royal Air Force to supply radar-jamming UAVs, completed a Tekever September 2026 raise of $580 million at a $6.4 billion valuation. Finland's ICEYE, which operates the world's largest commercial constellation of synthetic aperture radar (SAR) satellites — more than 70 spacecraft that can image any point on Earth regardless of cloud cover or darkness — has secured ICEYE defense contracts across several NATO nations and anchors Finland's $1.2 billion total for 2026. Germany's Stark Defence, which builds attack drones separate from Helsing's product line, executed a Stark Defence June 2026 raise of €500 million (approximately $562 million at current exchange rates).
ICEYE's SAR technology is worth briefly explaining, because it represents a different kind of European defense advantage than the drone sector. Traditional optical spy satellites are useless in cloud cover and darkness. Synthetic aperture radar uses microwave pulses and the motion of the satellite itself to synthesize the effect of a much larger antenna, producing detailed imagery under any weather conditions at any time of day. What ICEYE pioneered was miniaturizing SAR for defense applications to fit on small, inexpensive commercial satellites — reducing both unit cost and launch time dramatically compared with the billion-dollar military SAR platforms previously available only to major governments. The result is that NATO member nations can now buy persistent, all-weather surveillance capability as a commercial service rather than a decades-long procurement program.
Germany leads all European nations in defense venture funding for 2026 with $3.5 billion raised, followed by Finland at $1.2 billion and the United Kingdom at $932 million. The 27 EU member states collectively account for EU share of NATO defense VC at 21 percent of all NATO-wide defense VC funding, up from 15 percent at the same point in 2025, after funding more than doubled from $2.2 billion to $5.4 billion.
From Capital to Contracts: Where the System Still Breaks
Across the sector, investors and founders share a well-documented frustration: turning venture capital into military procurement is structurally harder in Europe than in the United States, and the scale of the current funding wave has not yet solved that problem.
The core issue is fragmentation. European defense procurement remains a national competence under Article 346 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, which allows member states to exempt defense contracts from competitive tendering rules on security grounds. Up to 80 percent of European defense procurement currently uses this exemption. Unlike US defense startups, which can pursue a single Department of Defense as their primary customer, a European company that wins a contract in Germany must essentially re-run a parallel sales cycle in France, Poland, Finland, and every other member state — each with its own requirements, certification standards, and procurement timelines. Israel is at risk of internal collapse or civil war because of tensions among Israelis, an August report by CIA experts tasked with providing “alternative analysis” said, according to a report by Drop Site News published on Monday.
The CIA report, titled “Fracture From Within", said that Israel faces a volatile situation ahead of 27 October elections, where Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu will be fighting for his political future.
The authors noted that one of the most divisive Israeli political issues is the long-standing exemption from military service that ultra-Orthodox Israelis enjoy.
The row has exposed deep divisions within Netanyahu's right-wing bloc and raised questions about whether he will have the support of two ultra-Orthodox parties: United Torah Judaism (UTJ) and Shas - his most dependable allies since he first became prime minister in 1996.
While hundreds of thousands of reservists have been mobilised for Israel’s genocide in Gaza and wars on Lebanon, Syria and Iran, ultra-Orthodox men have historically been exempt from compulsory military service in order to pursue full-time religious studies in yeshivas.
The arrangement has long been contentious, but the war has intensified pressure to end the exemption.
Netanyahu's coalition has repeatedly failed to pass legislation regulating ultra-Orthodox enlistment, leading to the detention of dozens of young men accused of evading military service and triggering mass protests backed by UTJ and Shas.
The report also noted that Israel faces tens of thousands of heavily armed veterans trying to assimilate back into civilian life. Israeli reservists can maintain their weapons at home, and carrying assault rifles in public is common in Israel.
Another factor that could drive instability in Israel is rising settler violence in the occupied West Bank and East Jerusalem, along with food inflation and the soaring cost of military spending, the report said.
Drop Site said that the CIA report was produced by the Red Cell, a semi-independent unit within the agency specifically designed to propose contrarian ideas and challenge basic assumptions and biases.
The report honed in on the pressures building ahead of an election that experts say may not produce a conclusive outcome. Polling in Israel suggests that neither Netanyahu nor the blocs opposed to him may reach the 61 seats required to form a government in parliament.
The authors also “gamed out” how these pressures could spark civil conflict. One precipitating event could be if foreign technology and AI companies limit their investments and hiring in Israel. Another would be if regional governments decided not to normalise or continue relations with Israel.
The article appeared to focus only on fissures among Israelis and did not take into account the tensions among Palestinian citizens of Israel, who account for 20 percent of the population and face discrimination.
On Friday, a Palestinian politician with Israeli citizenship dropped out of the upcoming parliamentary election after Israel’s Supreme Court suggested it would disqualify him from running. The court overturned bans on four other political parties of Palestinian citizens of Israel.

articles.title: Christa Pike’s lawyers had warned execution would be ‘difficult and perhaps cruel’ due to her veins - The Guardian
articles.summary: Christa Pike’s lawyers had warned execution would be ‘difficult and perhaps cruel’ due to her veins  The GuardianChrista Pike's prognosis still unclear after failed execution, lawyer says  BBCOpinion | I Consulted With Christa Pike’s Death Row Team. I Knew This Could Happen.  The New York TimesTennessee’s outgoing prison chief had a history of execution missteps before Christa Pike, officials say  cnn.comI interviewed Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pik...
articles.full_text:
A former lawyer for Christa Pike says he was not surprised that Tennessee botched its attempt to execute her because attorneys had warned that problems accessing her veins could make the procedure dangerous and potentially cruel.
James Crowson, who represented Pike during part of her post-conviction appeals, said he had followed the case from afar before the failed execution at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville on 30 September.
“Well, I can’t say I’m surprised,” said Crowson, who represented Pike while working for the Tennessee Post-Conviction Defender. “I knew that there were a number of defense filings saying that she had compromised veins, and that was going to be a difficult and perhaps cruel procedure for her because it was going to put her at risk for exactly what happened.”
Pike, 50, on Sunday remained hospitalized and on a machine helping her breathe after Tennessee administered two doses of pentobarbital that failed to kill her, as far as an attorney now representing her knew, the lawyer said on the CNN program State of the Union.
“She’s still in the hospital, on a ventilator, critically ill – we don’t really know the prognosis yet and may not know for several days,” Stephen Ferrell, an assistant federal defender, said to CNN host Jake Tapper.
Ferrell told Tapper that he had not been able to personally see Pike, but “this is the extent of what we know”.
Pike’s attorneys allege improperly placed intravenous lines allowed the drug with which she was injected to enter tissue rather than her bloodstream, leaving both arms severely injured.
The Tennessee Department of Correction has maintained that it followed every step of the state’s lawful execution protocol. And the department said the protocol did not permit additional procedures after the steps carried out on Wednesday.
Crowson said the accounts that officials followed the written protocol and that the execution was badly mishandled are not necessarily contradictory.
“The state comes up with a protocol and, typically, states that are inclined to impose the death penalty don’t really include medicine or science in the discussions when they’re coming up with these protocols,” he said.
Crowson said the reported injuries appeared consistent with the concerns raised before the execution, citing the theory that the drug entered surrounding tissue instead of circulating properly through Pike’s bloodstream.
Pike was sentenced to death for the 1995 torture and killing of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, a fellow student at the Knoxville Job Corps. Pike was 18 at the time. Her then boyfriend and co-defendant, Tadaryl Shipp, was 17 and was ineligible for the death penalty. He received a sentence of life imprisonment.
That gap in punishment based on a small age difference remains significant to Crowson. He said it illustrates what he views as the capricious nature of capital punishment.
“She’s a few months older than the young man that was engaged in the same conduct, and she’s been fighting for her life now for 32 years,” Crowson said. “He’s still in prison, but hasn’t been subjected to the death penalty.”
He said the age of 18 that was decisive for Pike “just seems like an arbitrary number”.
Crowson represented Pike during a stage of her post-conviction case about 16 years earlier and said he visited her “dozens of times” on death row. He said he last spoke with her in 2009.
He described Pike at the time as “very superficially charming” and attentive to people around her. But he said the person he knew bore little resemblance to the teenager whose crime sent her to death row.
“I never saw the Christa that committed those crimes that put her in prison,” Crowson said. “That person exists, obviously.”
The core of the post-conviction appeal, he said, was ineffective assistance of counsel. His team argued that Pike’s original attorneys failed to adequately present evidence about her mental illness, brain damage and history of severe childhood abuse during the sentencing phase.
Pike ultimately exhausted her appeals without ever getting relief, despite her attorneys’ offering evidence of being diagnosed with bipolar and post-traumatic stress disorders.
“It took me numerous years to even realize the gravity of what I’d done,” Pike had said in an earlier petition for clemency. “Even more to accept how many lives I affected. I took the life of someone’s child, sister, friend. It sickens me now to think I had the ability to commit such a crime.”
Crowson more recently said “there was a lot that was left out” at the time of Pike’s conviction.
“Would it have made a difference? I don’t know. There are a lot of people who feel very strongly, and her crime was grisly and horrifying.”
What happens next depends on whether Pike ultimately survives the botched execution – and, if she does, the extent of any lasting injuries.
Crowson said he expects intense pressure on Bill Lee, Tennessee’s governor, to commute Pike’s sentence to life imprisonment if she recovers. If she suffered serious neurological damage, he said, questions about her competency would become central to any attempt by Tennessee to execute her again.
The fallout of the botched execution widened on Saturday when Lee announced that Frank Strada, the Tennessee Department of Correction commissioner, would resign later in October. Lee has ordered an independent review and halted executions in the state for the remainder of the year.
Strada’s resignation was a predictable consequence of a botched execution now under national scrutiny, according to Crowson, who said: “Whenever you have a disaster like this, there’s going to be some fallout.”
Furthermore, Pike’s was at least the fifth execution Strada had botched since 2022 in Tennessee as well as Arizona, where he previously worked, according to death penalty lawyers.
Crowson said he hopes that Pike’s case results in the government taking a closer look at the death penalty as a functional legal punishment. He said there is a clear pattern between people who are sentenced to death and their history of trauma and mental illness not being accounted for during trial and sentencing.
“I think we as a nation have a strange relationship with mental illness,” he said. “It’s just so often discounted and mocked. It’s unfortunate.”

articles.title: Wars in Iran, Ukraine are driving an accelerated technology transfer between the CRINK allies - IntelliNews
articles.summary: Wars in Iran, Ukraine are driving an accelerated technology transfer between the CRINK allies  IntelliNews
articles.full_text:
Over the last four years North Korea and Iran have used military technology they are not supposed to have. In the first weeks of Operation Epic Fury IRGC missiles managed to destroy most of the US bases in the Gulf, dodging the nominally invincible THAAD and Patriot interceptors and have flown thousands of drones against Israel’s defences that somehow can evade electronic warfare jamming that was very effective only a year earlier.
North Korea’s ballistic missiles have also come on by leaps and bounds. Pyongyang test-fired a medium-range hypersonic missile on October 3 that it says uses an artificial intelligence module to change course mid-flight, effectively jumping sideways to avoid interceptors. Iran has used the same kind of weapon, something even America doesn’t have.
Iran also fired a North Korean designed ballistic missile at the US naval base Diego Garcia, 4,000km from its shores – twice the distance that military analysis previously assumed its rockets could reach - using Kheibar missiles based on North Korean designs.
The anti-Western CRINK alliance (China, Russia, Iran and North Korea) has been beefing up their game and sharing advanced military technology that in many areas, like hypersonic missiles, have the lead over the best that the West has to offer. And that has delivered unpleasant surprises in the asymmetrical war that has been unfolding on the shores of the Persian Gulf and the wheatfields of the Donbas.
North Korea the big winner
Of the allies, North Korea is probably the most backward. However, it has gained a boost from Russia particularly, which has been buying millions of artillery shells of Soviet-era stock to supplement its own supplies, particularly in the first year of the Ukrainian conflict, and paid with cash and military grade weapons technology as well as badly needed commodities. More recently, Kim Jong Un has sent a reported 50,000 troops to bolster Russian forces in the Ukrainian fields. Pyongyang is enjoying a boom as a result of the money flooding into the pariah state’s capital.
Kim Yo Jong, sister of leader Kim Jong-un and a department head in the ruling Workers' Party, said the missile's "wave trajectory mode" made it swerve erratically and drop off enemy radar. "In other words, this means it will be impossible to avoid an attack," she said, according to state news agency KCNA. Pyongyang says the system has four flight algorithms and an AI module that manoeuvres in real time, so that an interceptor such as the SM-3 or Patriot PAC-3 cannot calculate where to meet it.
South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff said the missile, launched from the Wonsan area, flew "more than 700 km"; Japan's defence ministry said about 680 km. North Korea claims 1,000 km and says the gap shows the allied radars lost the missile. If that is true, a manoeuvring hypersonic weapon with that range puts the US and Japanese naval bases at Sasebo and Iwakuni within reach, and possibly Guam. It is also possible Pyongyang is dressing up a failed flight as a breakthrough.
Drone tech boost
Already the technology is flowing back the other way as Russia is sharing its recently battle-tested innovations with its CRINK partners.
The test came a day before President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said Russia had shared its new jet-powered drone technology with North Korea. Initially Russia bought the kamikaze Shahed drones in large numbers from Iran at the start of the Ukraine war, but in 2025 it did a technology transfer deal with Tehran and built a vast drone factory in the Alabuga Special Economic Zone in Tatarstan. Since then it has poured money into development and recently retired its Geran-2 and -3 drones, prop-driven models based on the Iranian-designed Shahed-136 loitering munition and replaced them with the much more advanced Geran-4 jet powered version as well as the cruise-missile light Geran-5 and Banderol missiles both of which can outrun Ukraine’s new interceptor missiles, drastically reducing Ukraine’s interception rates.
Asked whether Moscow had passed on this technology at a press conference last week, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said: "Yes, of course. They're sharing with North Korea all the technologies." He said he believed Russia was also helping with ballistic missiles, "because North Korea helped them with missiles. It's a very dangerous moment."
There is also hard evidence of Russia transferring air-defence and electronic-warfare technology to North Korea, according to the 11-country Multilateral Sanctions Monitoring Team in May last year. Russia has supplied North Korea with at least one Pantsir mobile air-defence system, a Pantsir-class combat vehicle and electronic-warfare jamming equipment after North Korean troops began deploying to Russia. South Korea's national security adviser separately said Russia had supplied anti-aircraft missiles and equipment and was assisting Pyongyang's satellite programme.
Experts say that Ukraine is being used by Pyongyang as a live-fire R&D laboratory for North Korean missiles, according to analysis by 38 North which examined the North Korean- made KN-23 missiles Russia has fired in Ukraine; early missiles reportedly suffered accuracy and reliability problems; later examples performed significantly better.
China is doing the same thing: Russia's IEMZ Kupol working with Chinese specialists in China to develop and flight-test the Garpiya-3/G3 long-range attack drone, Reuters reported, and sample Chinese-produced drones have repeatedly been found on the battlefield in Ukraine. Separately, a Center for Strategic & International Studies (CSIS) study also found China and Hong Kong to be important sources of drone-engine components, electronics and manufacturing equipment used by Iran and Russia.
That is a problem for Ukraine as it heads into a winter campaign that was always going to be brutal. Ukraine has also been pouring money into development and has developed jet-powered interceptor missiles and reportedly used its home-grown FP-7 ballistic missiles against a Russian target for the first time last week.
But Russia's missile arsenal is already growing far faster than Ukraine's air defences, as Kyiv’s interceptor stocks run dry, and Russia has been supplementing its own stockpile of a reported 130 ballistic missiles with North Korean made munitions. A week earlier Zelenskiy warned that Moscow was also preparing to recruit another 10,000 North Korean military personnel to fight in Ukraine during what is widely expected to be a devasting winter campaign.
Russia aiding Iran
The exchange is part of a wider transfer of weapons technology between the members of the informal CRINK bloc which the Iran war has pushed into an open closer military cooperation.
Iran’s drone technology has improved remarkably in just a year since its last exchange with Israel in 2025. Russia is apparently helping Iran develop supersonic cruise missiles the Financial Times reported in September after an investigation uncovered a covert programme called C430L, running since 2023, involving Rosoboronexport and Russia's NPO Mashinostroyenia.
Leaked correspondence, travel records and military patents showed Russian engineers analysing Iranian ramjet flight-test telemetry and advising on fuel delivery, combustion stability, air intakes and engine nozzles. In April 2025 Rosoboronexport proposed sending roughly two dozen Russian specialists to Iran for technical consultations, the paper reported, and the programme was still active in 2026.
This is not simply selling Tehran a missile: it is transferring the knowledge needed for Iran eventually to design and manufacture its own supersonic anti-ship and land-attack weapons that can match anything the US has.
And it’s not just materiel they are sharing. In September Pyongyang ran its first exercise mixing attack drones with missiles, rockets and artillery against a single target, borrowing tactics Russia has gleaned from its campaign in Ukraine and the Middle East.
The Iran war highlights how far this cooperation has gone. Iran fielded a hypersonic missile, a technology the US does not yet have, and its missiles repeatedly penetrated Patriot defences. In a stunning development by late March US troops had been forced out of all 13 of their Gulf bases, the backbone of the US security umbrella for the region, most of them left all but uninhabitable, according to The New York Times.
Iranian drones have also become a lot more effective after it abandoned GPS after its 12-day war with Israel in 2025 and switched to China’s BeiDou satellite navigation system, which improved accuracy and helped its drones beat Israeli electronic warfare. Russia has in turn supplied Iran back with its own innovative drone technology advances developed at Alabuga, along with satellite intelligence, during its war with the US and Israel.
Sanctions force Russia to innovate
Beyond weapons, sanctions have forced Russia to build what it used to import, and China has been its main supplier. It started with cheese, after Putin banned the import of European agricultural products in 2014; almost all the high quality cheese on Russian shelves was imported from Europe, but as the shelves cleared within two years, Russia was forced to bootstrap a domestic cheese industry that have subsequently flourish.
More challengingly, Siemens had a near-monopoly on high-efficiency gas turbines for Russian power plants until it left in 2022; Power Machines is now shipping its own 155 MW GTE-170.1 turbines and United Engine Corporation is testing a 25 MW industrial model that is reportedly on a par with the best German machines.

articles.full_text:
The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has added a critical Citrix NetScaler vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-88779, to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog after confirming evidence of active exploitation.
The flaw affects Citrix NetScaler ADC (formerly Citrix ADC) and Citrix NetScaler Gateway (formerly Citrix Gateway).
CVE-2026-88779 is an improper restriction of operations within the bounds of a memory buffer vulnerability, classified under CWE-119.
CISA Warns of Citrix NetScaler Flaw
Such weaknesses can occur when software does not adequately validate memory operations, potentially allowing an attacker to trigger a denial-of-service condition against vulnerable appliances.
CISA added the vulnerability to the KEV Catalog on October 4, 2026, and set an October 7, 2026 remediation deadline for impacted federal civilian executive branch agencies.
The accelerated timeline underscores the operational risk of internet-facing NetScaler infrastructure, which is often deployed to provide remote access, application delivery, VPN connectivity, and identity-related gateway services.
While CISA’s entry does not identify ransomware use or publicly disclose technical exploitation details, the agency’s KEV designation confirms the vulnerability has been exploited in real-world attacks.
The listing also requires forensic triage under Binding Operational Directive 26-04, indicating that organizations should not treat patching as the sole response where affected systems may have been exposed.
Administrators should immediately identify all exposed NetScaler ADC and Gateway instances, including devices hosted in cloud environments or managed through third parties.
Organizations should then apply Citrix-provided mitigations and security updates in line with vendor instructions. CISA said entities that cannot mitigate the issue should stop using the affected product until protections are available.
Security teams should also review appliance logs, authentication records, administrative activity, configuration changes, and unusual network connections for signs of compromise.
Because NetScaler devices often sit at the network edge and handle authentication or traffic-routing functions, successful exploitation can cause availability issues and may give attackers an opportunity to target high-value access infrastructure.
The advisory directs stakeholders to assess each asset’s internet exposure and follow the risk-based patching and forensic-triage requirements outlined in BOD 26-04.
Private-sector organizations are not bound by the directive, but CISA’s KEV inclusion strongly indicates the vulnerability should be treated as urgent.

CNN’s global affairs analyst Brett McGurk is out with a book tomorrow, Brink:  Inside the Race to Free the October 7th Hostages, a firsthand account of the Gaza hostage negotiations and the wider Middle East crisis that followed October 7.
The following excerpt details the beginnings of the unlikely cooperation between the outgoing Biden administration and Trump’s incoming team to secure a Gaza hostage-and-ceasefire deal. It offers an inside-the-room account of how political rivals tried to turn a narrow diplomatic opening into an agreement before the transfer of power.
Secure rooms in the US Capitol are cavernous compared to the White House Situation Room. They are designed for full committees or larger gatherings, not intimate discussions. On Nov. 20, 2024, Jake Sullivan and I had gone to one of those rooms to brief our successors two weeks after Donald Trump resoundingly defeated Kamala Harris.
Sullivan was Biden’s national security advisor. His named successor was Mike Waltz, a congressman from Florida. I was Biden’s lead on the Middle East and a chief negotiator on talks to free hostages held by Hamas in Gaza in exchange for a ceasefire with Israel. My named successor was Steve Witkoff — a real-estate tycoon and Trump’s best friend.
Shortly after the election, I had called Jared Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law and former Middle East hand. My message was that we had a chance to secure a Gaza deal so long as we could be seen as working together without any daylight between the incoming and outgoing teams. That was a tall order given the polarization in Washington, but it was the only chance we had — and for the first time in months, circumstances trended in our favor.
The hostage talks had collapsed in August, when shortly after Biden, together with the leaders of Egypt and Qatar, presented a new proposal endorsed by Israel, Hamas terrorists murdered six hostages in a tunnel under Rafah, a city in southern Gaza. One of those hostages was Hersh Goldberg-Polin, an American who had been grievously wounded and lost an arm in Hamas’s attacks at the Nova music festival on Oct. 7, 2023, before being taken captive.
Following the collapse of the negotiations, Israel had won a string of military victories. It started on Sept. 17, 2024, with an operation that exploded thousands of beepers carried by Hezbollah militants in Lebanon. I first heard about what became known as Operation Grim Beeper from a contact in Mossad, Israel’s external intelligence service, who told me, “We just blew the dicks off Hezbollah.”
In many cases, that was not metaphorical.
Hezbollah, like Hamas, a terrorist group backed by Iran, had made the fateful decision to join in the Hamas attack on Israel. On Oct. 8, 2023, it began firing daily rocket barrages into northern Israel, eventually displacing nearly 80,000 people. Israel had been prepared to forgo an operation against Hezbollah if there was a hostage deal. But with no deal in sight, Israel soon followed the beeper operation with a ground assault into the Hezbollah strongholds of southern Lebanon.
By the end of September, Hezbollah’s leader, Hassan Nasrallah, was dead, together with most of his senior lieutenants, buried in an underground Beirut compound.
On Oct. 1, following Nasrallah’s death, Iran made its own foolish — and fateful — decision to launch another massive ballistic missile attack against Israel, following on a failed attack it had launched months earlier. This time, Iran launched nearly two hundred missiles at once, exceeding its earlier salvo.
In the Situation Room that afternoon, as interceptors destroyed incoming missiles at the edge of outer space, we received reports of a direct hit on a college dormitory in Tel Aviv. I was seated just across from Harris, less than five weeks from Election Day. She mouthed, “Oh, shit.” We knew that if Iran inflicted significant Israeli casualties, the Israelis were prepared to launch a massive counterattack into Iran.
Fortunately, that report, like many first reports, was wrong. Only remnants of a destroyed missile struck the building, causing little damage. The attack was mostly defeated, dismaying the Iranians, who had believed their larger salvo of missiles would be successful.
About two weeks later, on Oct. 16, Israeli forces killed Hamas’s leader, Yahya Sinwar. He was found in Rafah, not far from where Hersh and five other hostages had been shot to death in a tunnel. Sinwar’s death removed a major obstacle to a deal — him — and allowed the Israelis to be more flexible on some terms now that the mastermind of the Oct. 7 attacks could no longer reclaim power. For Israel, it was akin to the United States military killing Osama bin Laden after 9/11.
Finally, on Oct. 26, Israel conducted stealth air attacks against Iran, targeting and destroying many of its strategic air defense systems. We worked closely with the Israelis on this counterattack, walking the Israelis back from a more aggressive response.
Biden told Netanyahu that we would deploy more air defenses to Israel and received assurance from Netanyahu in return that Israel’s response would focus on Iran’s own air defense batteries. The aim was to change the balance of power without triggering a wider war. We messaged Iran’s leaders afterward that their country was now wide open to air attacks should Israel (or the United States) choose to launch them. With Russia bogged down in Ukraine, Iran could not soon replace the destroyed air defense batteries, most of which were Russian and had proved ineffective against Israel’s capabilities. Iran never responded to Israel’s counterattack.
With the tables turned on Iran, Sinwar dead, and Hezbollah’s leadership decimated, we predicted that Hezbollah would soon accept a ceasefire deal with Israel. That would be the moment to return to the Gaza deal — picking up where we had left off in August.
My case to Kushner was straightforward. If Israel and Hamas knew that Trump would implement the deal on the table, we had a chance to close it before he took office. But if not, we would lose the best chance we had had since the war began. It was time to seize the moment, and the only way to do that was by working together.
Kushner fully agreed.
He told me that he would not be joining the new administration but said my successor on the Middle East was someone close to Trump, a pragmatic problem-solver who would want to work with me to the extent appropriate. He did not mention Witkoff, whose name emerged days later as Trump’s likely Middle East envoy.
Biden invited Trump to the Oval on Nov. 13, 2024, mostly for a one-on-one. When the cameras came in briefly, Biden promised a smooth transition. “Politics is tough,” Trump said. “And it’s in many cases not a very nice world, but it is a nice world today, and I appreciate very much a transition that is so smooth, it’ll be as smooth as it can get.”
I saw Biden afterward. Unlike many Democrats at the time who saw the election as an existential disaster, Biden — at least with me — was focused on working with the incoming team wherever we could. That was especially so on the hostage crisis.
According to Biden, the two presidents agreed to coordinate, setting the stage for my meeting with Sullivan, Waltz, and Witkoff seven days later.
In the secure room at the Capitol, Sullivan snapped open a document pouch and arrayed briefing materials in front of him, including maps of the region and background on Iran’s nuclear program. We sat alone at a large table, waiting for Trump’s team to arrive.
Waltz entered, followed by Witkoff. The former was a retired military officer with perfect hair and rod-straight posture. The latter was a brash real estate developer known for carrying a pistol in a sock through the alleys and streets of New York, where he built a multibillion-dollar empire. Both exhibited a lighthearted manner, something that I had lost handling the Gaza crisis, where tens of thousands had died, over one hundred hostages remained in tunnels underground and the region stood on the brink of an all-out war.
The meeting began awkwardly, the four of us standing at the corner of the large table in the oversize room, introducing ourselves by titles. Waltz took his seat, and we followed.
“Trump told us to solve everything, that’s our mission,” Witkoff said, laughing.
“Solve it!” Waltz added.
Senator JD Vance, the incoming vice president, popped in unexpectedly. We stood. He asked what we were talking about, and when we said the Middle East, he told us that was his cue to leave. (Run as fast as you can, I thought.) Vance, Waltz, and Witkoff discussed recent calls they’d each had with Trump, comparing notes on what they had heard — apparently different things. The calls had come at all hours, and Waltz asked both men whether Trump ever slept. Witkoff answered, “I’ve known him for forty years, the answer is — no, not very much.”
“Force of nature,” Waltz remarked.
Witkoff explained that he had been Trump’s real-estate attorney before branching out on his own. “I’ve had success, but there’s only one Trump,” he told us. Vance came around the table to shake my hand, and Sullivan’s. He said he wanted to work with us during the transition period, which seemed sincere, and then left the room.
With a map on the table, Sullivan walked through what had changed in the Middle East since the hostage talks collapsed in August. It was head-spinning even for those of us who had been living and breathing the issues every day since then. For Witkoff, I recounted my difficult experience on the hostage talks, and explained why we might now, finally, have a shot.
Of course, for that to happen we had to be seen — by both Hamas and Israel — as working together, as both parties would demand to know Trump’s views.
“The only reason I’m here is to save lives,” Witkoff said. “It’s the most noble thing anyone can do with their life, to save another life. So, I’m all in, count on it.”
