articles.title: China’s Long Twilight
articles.summary: Demographic decline, political paralysis, and the fate of great powers.
articles.full_text:
During the boom years of the reform era, from 1978 to the early 2000s, China was a country of productive workers. The working-age population (those aged 15 to 64) rose from 57 percent of the population in 1978 to a peak of nearly 75 percent in 2010. They built the roads, factories, apartment complexes, and firms that powered three decades of close to ten percent annual growth—a 20-fold economic expansion.
But over the past decade, this tide has turned. Beijing’s one-child policy, plus the same social forces that have dragged East Asian fertility to historic lows, have produced below-replacement birth rates for three decades in China—draining the fuel that powered China’s rise. China’s total population peaked at 1.4 billion in 2021 and is now falling by three to four million people per year—roughly equivalent to losing one Los Angeles each year. By the 2040s, if China continues to follow East Asia’s descent to ultralow fertility rates, it will shed around one percent of its population annually—roughly ten million people, more than the population of New York City. At the same time, the proportion of China’s population aged 65 and older will surge, doubling from 15 percent today to around 30 percent in the 2040s, and then rising to well over 40 percent by the late twenty-first century. The size of that cohort in the United States, by contrast, is projected to rise far more gradually, from around 19 percent of the population today to just over 23 percent in 2060.
Put simply, China is entering a century of demographic decline. This change will remake the country’s economy and politics just as dramatically as the last century’s demographic boom did. Back in the mid-twentieth century, improvements in health and falling infant mortality rates led to a burgeoning youth population, which Mao Zedong channeled into revolutionary social change, overturning entrenched hierarchies and remaking society from the bottom up. By 1978, China had a swelling population of working-age adults, and Chinese leader Deng Xiaoping’s pragmatic policies of “reform and opening up” astutely plugged them into the global economy, allowing China to emerge as the world’s factory.
Today, as the population rapidly grays, China’s political system is becoming increasingly regressive and rigid. As the Chinese Communist Party pivots back toward one-man rule, its vaunted institutions of technocratic rule are not what they once were. Instead of creatively addressing emerging challenges, the CCP is relying on repression and reflexively following central mandates—no matter the risks. Economically, for instance, policymakers continue to pursue Chinese leader Xi Jinping’s preferred export-driven industrial policy despite the obvious need to boost domestic consumption and strengthen the social security net for the poor.
The story of twenty-first-century China, then, is not just one of demographic decline but also one of political paralysis—and what happens when those two intersect. It is this combination that makes China’s future especially bleak. As China ages, the social pressures bearing down on its political system will only intensify. Mid-twenty-first-century China could end up looking a lot like the sixteenth-century Ming dynasty, a sclerotic political regime rendered increasingly brittle by worsening social, gender, and generational divides. Lest observers in Washington gloat about this fate, however, China’s trajectory is ultimately a warning: demographic decline and political erosion can hollow out any great power—including the United States.
The Politics of Paralysis
As the journalist Li Yuan has observed, the United States suffers from China envy. Tech investors fawn over its latest AI models. Energy specialists are awestruck by its industrial dominance in batteries and solar power. And journalists and analysts often return from visits offering rosy-eyed panegyrics about China’s gleaming transit systems and engineering capacity. Politicians and pundits, meanwhile, often fuse China’s expanding navy and missile tests with Xi’s speeches on “the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation” to form a single image: a strong state successfully executing a grand strategy for its twenty-first-century rise.
Compared with the political circus in Washington and the malaise in the rest of America, such surface-level manifestations of China’s wealth and power often lead to sweeping conclusions about relative national trajectories. But on closer inspection, Beijing is also undergoing profound political erosion—it just doesn’t look like the process playing out in Washington. Because China’s system is tightly controlled, its descent into personalistic one-man rule does not play out in divisive confrontations on television or erratic social media rants by the top leader. Beijing’s transformation is instead happening quietly but just as consequentially. Over the past two decades, the CCP has come to revolve ever more tightly around a single man. Xi successfully lifted the constitutional term limits on his rule as state president in 2018 and swept clean the top ranks of the party itself at the 20th Party Congress, in 2022, packing them with his own supporters and yes men. Similar purges have regularly rocked the top ranks of China’s military, culminating in 2026, with the removal of Zhang Youxia, Xi’s own handpicked top general, leaving Xi virtually alone at the helm of China’s armed services.
Xi is now set to assume a fourth five-year term as party general secretary in 2027 and has given no sign as to who might take his place in 2032, when he will be 79 years old. An aged, isolated leader increases the risks of policy missteps in China, just as it does in the United States. But China’s slide from an efficient technocratic state into lifetime rule under an aging autocrat underscores a fundamental reality about the two countries’ trajectories: unlike China, the United States can still choose differently—in the midterm elections, in 2028, and every few years thereafter. China’s politics, by contrast, are far more stagnant.
 By the 2040s, China could lose ten million people a year.
Most critically, the stifling political atmosphere Xi has created is draining Beijing’s ability to respond to emerging problems as earlier generations once did. Back in the 1970s and 1980s, Chinese leaders under Deng were able to kickstart China’s era of rapid growth through rural reforms that completely reworked Maoist economic orthodoxy. As Zhao Shukai, a key party official involved in those reforms, has noted, Beijing’s ability to do so depended on a degree of “openness in the political structure, both in top-level power relations and in the ideological sphere.” That same era of flexibility saw party leaders empower competent and efficient officials to boldly address other pressing economic challenges, such as when General Secretary Jiang Zemin charged Premier Zhu Rongji with overhauling the tax system in 1994 to put China’s central finances on a firmer footing.
As Chinese politics regress, such flexible problem solving is giving way to rigid orthodoxy. Cadres now find themselves pressed to dogmatically pursue Xi’s signature policies regardless of the consequences. Back in 2022, for instance, Shanghai officials under Li Qiang, then municipal party secretary, abandoned their tentative efforts at a lighter, targeted approach to handling the spreading Omicron variant of COVID-19 when it became clear that such a policy would conflict with the “zero COVID” policies on which Xi had staked his personal legitimacy. The result was a brutal, two-month lockdown of Shanghai that left many without reliable access to food and medicine, and which became the template for lockdowns throughout China later that year. Rather than being censured for the debacle, however, Li was elevated by Xi to the top ranks of the Politburo Standing Committee in 2022 and made state premier in 2023. He now loyally leads Chinese officials on Xi’s push for industrial manufacturing and an export-driven growth strategy, despite concerns from economists about deflation, mounting overcapacity, and declining consumption.
Xi is not solely responsible for the stultifying inertia that is spreading in China’s society and state. Ever since the “color revolutions” of the early 2000s in post-Soviet states and the Arab Spring in 2010, party elites have grown more fearful of social unrest. Chinese authorities have tightened their grip on the media, the legal profession, and civil society, limiting the space for Chinese citizens to discuss mounting social woes and extinguishing emerging calls for deeper political reform. Space within the ranks of the CCP itself has similarly constricted, with few now willing to consider reforms that might seriously affect the vested interests of entrenched social groups. Back in the 1990s, by contrast, Zhu pushed through the wrenching restructuring of state-owned enterprises to secure China’s 2001 entry into the World Trade Organization—even though it threw tens of millions out of work and fueled massive labor protests. Accepting such short-term pain in pursuit of long-term gain was once considered one of China’s defining advantages, but Beijing today shows little comparable appetite for such measures.
Consider the party’s hesitancy in addressing the financial ramifications of China’s demographic decline. For decades, China’s retirement ages were among the lowest in the world: 60 years old for men, 55 for white-collar women, and 50 for blue-collar women. Unsurprisingly, Chinese researchers have predicted that the main urban pension fund covering some 500 million urban workers, retirees, and cadres will be exhausted by the mid-2030s. Raising the retirement age has thus been on Beijing’s to-do list for well over a decade. Yet authorities have moved extraordinarily slowly and timidly. articles.title: The Triumph of Tech-Fueled Propaganda
articles.summary: America isn’t ready for the next wave of foreign influence operations.
articles.full_text:
In April and May, hundreds of users of the social media platform Bluesky discovered that their accounts had been hijacked and used to spread content about Ukraine. Researchers at Clemson University later attributed the campaign to the Social Design Agency, a Russian consulting firm sanctioned by the U.S. Department of Treasury for running Kremlin-directed malign influence campaigns. The Bluesky effort turned out to be only one piece of the SDA’s much larger portfolio of recent operations: leaked documents obtained by the news portal Delfi Estonia and shared with the Organized Crime and Corruption Reporting Project revealed plans for real-world acts of vandalism, intimidation, and election interference.
Most discussions of online influence and disinformation campaigns assume that attacks such as the one on Bluesky are discrete efforts. But as the SDA’s operations show, influence operations are increasingly interconnected and part of propaganda strategies that transcend traditional boundaries. Sophisticated states such as China, Iran, and Russia routinely combine overt public messaging with covert influence and mix broadcast channels with social media platforms. State media outlets, official government accounts, paid influencers, fake personas, hacked accounts, and bot armies are parts of the same system. This integrated approach, which we call “full-spectrum propaganda,” is now the norm for U.S. adversaries trying to spread their message abroad.
In full-spectrum propaganda, as we outlined in a recent Security Studies article, the many channels that states can use reinforce each other, making narratives seem more credible and allowing them to proliferate more widely. A story publicized on a state-backed broadcast channel may reach one audience, while social media accounts catch the attention of another. Official outlets can quote from posts on fake accounts whose creators masquerade as ordinary members of the public, making a fringe claim seem normal. Paid influencers can tailor messages in a style that resonates with niche audiences. The rapid expansion of artificial intelligence is making this strategy even more powerful: states are increasingly integrating AI into every level of their propaganda operations, allowing small groups or individuals to conduct propaganda campaigns that would previously have required far greater resources.
Strategies that merely address discrete foreign influence campaigns will fail to meet the challenges presented by full-spectrum propaganda. The United States needs to be able to understand, assess, and counter influence operations holistically, yet as the threat grows, the United States has been undercutting the capacity that would allow it to do so. Politicians have been dismantling the government agencies designed to track foreign influence, and social media companies are raising barriers to research on their platforms, leaving the country unprepared. As AI accelerates the spread and expands the reach of global propaganda, Washington is blinding itself to the challenge.
EVERYTHING EVERYWHERE ALL AT ONCE
For much of the last decade, politicians and the public understood foreign influence operations on social media through the parts that first became visible. Most often, this would be a network of fake accounts discovered by social media companies as part of their efforts to eliminate bots, scams, and online deception on their platforms. After taking down such accounts, companies would write reports and researchers (including us) would publish analyses to explain the evolving tactics, techniques, and procedures of online influence campaigns. The focus on the specifics of each individual operation led people to think of the threats as narrow, distinct incidents.
But the fragment of what is visible is not the whole story. State-backed propagandists do not have to choose between state media and fake accounts, between covert personas and overt broadcasters, or between a spoofed media outlet or a Telegram channel. They can use all of them together—and they are increasingly doing so.
The SDA, for instance, documented its own work in the style of a consultancy reporting to a client. That client, the leaked documents suggest, was the administration of Russian President Vladimir Putin, whose officials appear in the agency’s internal communications overseeing its work. The consulting firm’s covert operations are just one component of a much broader Russian propaganda apparatus that also includes state media networks, official government channels, and fake personas. Moscow and its proxies use all of these tools in tandem to amplify propaganda messages and reach many types of audiences.
 Looking at foreign influence campaigns as a social media problem is too limited.
As the Organized Crime and Corruption Reporting Project and other news outlets explained, the SDA was behind a fake video in June 2025, branded to appear as if it were made by the Saudi media outlet Al Arabiya, which claimed that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky purchased a luxury apartment in Burj Khalifa, a skyscraper in Dubai. An internal report estimated that this false story could have logged as many as 86 million views globally; a similar SDA effort targeting Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan likely racked up over ten million views. In some cases, rather than mimicking an existing outlet such as Al Arabiya, SDA conjures fully branded fake news outlets: one leaked document described plans to use an outlet tied to the SDA in Armenia’s June parliamentary elections.
When more distance is required, SDA turns to paid influencers. Earlier this year, for example, the Kremlin wanted to support the reelection bid of Viktor Orban, then Hungary’s prime minister. According to the Financial Times, the SDA, recognizing that overt support from Russia could be interpreted as foreign meddling and hurt Orban’s campaign, proposed contacting local influencers via go-betweens to make the Russian content appear homegrown.
The SDA even bridges the gap between the real world and online information by staging controversial or threatening events to generate attention. In September 2025, severed pig heads, including several marked “Macron” for the French president, were left outside mosques and Islamic centers in and around Paris. The leaked SDA files reveal the meticulous plans behind the effort, along with similar vandalism plots elsewhere in France and in Germany. Mainstream broadcast and social media covered these events, generating real-world concern about xenophobia and Islamophobia in Europe. The SDA calls these “cognitive strikes”: the point is securing visibility, shaping perceptions, and creating emotional responses that can be exploited.
Such covert activity complements Moscow’s efforts to continue to develop its broadcast propaganda apparatus worldwide. In 2025, the Kremlin allocated 31 billion rubles ($367 million) to RT, the Russian state broadcaster. RT and Sputnik, the state news agency and radio service, have expanded across Africa, Latin America, the Middle East, and Southeast Asia, according to the BBC, including by taking over local media channels. RT Academy, the broadcaster’s educational arm, ran a journalism program in Jakarta, the Indonesian capital, to train a new generation of reporters; its programming included “fact checking” and “applying ethical standards” in storytelling. RT is not only broadcasting on its own stations but is also funding and operating sympathetic proxy channels. In 2024, for example, the U.S. Department of Justice indicted two RT employees for funneling nearly $10 million to Tenet Media, a right-wing U.S. media outlet. Even influencers working for Tenet Media were unaware of the source of that funding.
A CONFLUENCE OF INFLUENCE
Full-spectrum propaganda presents a distinct challenge because it exploits the way modern information systems confer legitimacy. As research in psychology has shown, repetition reinforces belief, and a narrative may seem more believable when it appears in multiple distinct places or when many seemingly unconnected people start talking about it. A claim looks more credible when an outlet, a few influencers, and some individuals in a Telegram channel seem to arrive at the same conclusion independently.
Integrated propaganda campaigns can also more easily evade existing crackdown efforts by individual platforms. Because social media companies differ in how they regulate content, when fake accounts on one site get removed, they may simply respawn or migrate to platforms with more permissible policies or weaker enforcement capacity. When Russian officials and state media outlets portrayed the bombing of a Ukrainian maternity hospital in March 2022 as a faked event and claimed that the victims were paid actors, social media platforms such as Twitter took down the deceptive content. But anonymous Telegram channels claiming to be fact-checking organizations gained popularity and spread the false narrative there. Some of these efforts may have been genuine attempts to investigate the charges, but many others appeared to be the work of state-backed propaganda groups seeking new places to share their message.
In a world of full-spectrum propaganda, then, looking at foreign influence campaigns on a platform-by-platform basis or simply as a social media problem is too limited. Merely analyzing posts on Bluesky, for instance, overlooks the way the message they are promoting connects to simultaneous efforts on Facebook and X, articles in state media, and public broadcasts around the world. Understanding a modern propaganda campaign requires examining where else a narrative may have appeared, whether fake outlets were quoted by influencers, whether ostensibly independent sources were connected, and how those different parts of the system reinforce one another.
